problem: Multi-object navigation methods over-focus on local path optimization, converging slowly under sparse rewards and risking deadlocks or traps. Independently optimized subtasks give redundant, overlapping paths instead of cross-task optimization in a shared decision space.
motivation: MON requires sequentially finding multiple targets under incomplete information, so the agent must balance immediate actions against long-term reward. The authors argue the core difficulty is deformation of the shared decision space, so path planning should be optimized dynamically across tasks rather than by aggregating subtasks.
key_idea: Combine target-specific value losses into one objective and adjust their weights dynamically by gradient-based updates, normalized by per-target navigation success rate so harder targets get priority.
insight: Only the abstract was available, so no ablation evidence can be cited. The abstract suggests that success-rate-normalized adaptive weighting prevents over-optimization on easy targets, and that it addresses sparse rewards and improves convergence efficiency. Prior-knowledge navigation and frontier-aware exploration are described as auxiliary modules that add further gains.
method: GDWO: merges target-specific value loss functions into one optimization framework and updates their weights by gradient-based adjustment.
Success-rate weight normalization: during training, weights are normalized according to per-target navigation success rates to prevent over-optimization and prioritize harder targets.
Prior knowledge-based navigation: auxiliary module that uses prior knowledge to guide navigation.
Frontier-aware exploration: auxiliary module that guides exploration toward frontiers to reduce exploration cost.

setting.backbone: not specified in abstract (RL-trained navigation policy)
setting.training_data: not specified in abstract; trained on Gibson and Matterport3D

results: The abstract reports only that GDWO improves key MON metrics on Gibson and Matterport3D, optimizing path planning, reducing exploration cost and improving navigation efficiency. No numbers or baselines are given.
limitations: Only the abstract was available, so quantitative results and details cannot be verified.
The method likely depends on the design of the auxiliary modules and on success-rate statistics during training.
